question: Is there a provision for a State Spatial Planning Board which is mandated with planning policies and reforms for the state?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Partly answered. The Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961 does provide for a State Town-Planning Board. But section 4 only enables it: the State Government "may" set it up by notification. It is not a "shall" provision. Under the methodology, a "may" provision earns Part A only if the Board has actually been set up by a government notification or order, or this is shown on an official state department website. No such notification, order or website is in the Citation Sheet, so Part A cannot be decided. If Part A were met, Part B would be supported: s.4 gives the Board a stated mandate to advise the State on planning and development and to set principles and policies for the State as a whole. | EVIDENCE: (1) KTCP Act 1961, s.4 (ULG-02, PRS compilation, p.21-22): "The State Government may, by notification, constitute a State Town-Planning Board for the State ... for advising the State Government regarding planning and development and for determining principles and policies for achieving the balanced development of the State as a whole." (2) s.2(1a): "'Board' means the State Town Planning Board constituted under this Act". (3) The Act also says the State Government must consult "the Board" before amalgamating or sub-dividing planning areas (s.4A(3)), framing schemes for funds and assets (s.4A(5), s.4B(2)(ii)) and setting up Planning Authorities (s.4C(1)). These sections assume a Board exists, but they do not prove it was ever set up. (4) s.3 makes appointing a D

State Town-Planning Board. —The State Government may, by notification, constitute a State Town-Planning Board for the State with such members and in such manner as may be prescribed for advising the State Government regarding planning and development and for determining principles and policies for achieving the balanced development of the State as a whole.

provision: Section 4 (State Town-Planning Board); see also s.2(1a), s.4A(3), s.4A(5), s.4B(2)(ii), s.4C(1)
clause: s.4 (whole section)
comments:
Part A is left blank because the evidence is not found, not because the Board is absent. Section 4 of the Karnataka Town and Country Planning (KTCP) Act 1961 (ULG-02, PRS compilation, amended up to Act 38 of 2015) only enables a State Town-Planning Board: the State Government "may, by notification, constitute" it. It is not a 'shall' provision. The methodology says a 'may' provision earns Part A only if a government notification or order, or an official department or planning-body website, shows the Board was actually set up. No such notification, order or web page is in the Citation Sheet. Other sections require consulting "the Board": s.4A(3) and (5), s.4B(2)(ii) and s.4C(1). Section 2(1a) defines the Board as "constituted under this Act". These sections assume a Board exists but do not prove it was set up, so they are not enough. I did not score NO, because there is no affirmative absence: the Board may well exist and the sheet simply lacks the proof.

What I checked: KTCP Act sections 2(1a), 3, 4, 4A-4H and 51 (ULG-02). Section 3 (the Director of Town Planning, a 'shall' duty) is an official, not a board. Section 51 Joint Town Planning Boards are local bodies, not a state-level body. I also checked the KTCP Amendment Bill 2025 (ULG-03). It creates a Commissionerate and Commissioner (new ss.2A-2B) and makes the Greater Bengaluru Authority the planning authority (new s.81-G). It leaves s.4 unchanged and does not say the Board exists. It is also a Bill: its commencement depends on a notification, which is not in the sheet. I found nothing relevant in the Greater Bengaluru Governance Act 2024 (ULG-01), the GBG Amendment Bill (ULG-05), the BBMP Act 2020 (ULG-19), the BDA Act (ULG-04), the BMLTA Act (ULG-18) or the BMRDA pages (ULG-10/20/21). A sheet-wide search for 'State Town Planning Board' returned only ULG-02.

Part B = YES. Section 4 explicitly gives the Board the job of "advising the State Government regarding planning and development and for determining principles and policies for achieving the balanced development of the State as a whole". That is a state-level planning-policy mandate. The word 'reforms' is not used, but under the scorer notes the Board's functions match the intent of the question. Per the column, Part B counts only if Part A = YES.

To confirm: find the notification or GO constituting the State Town-Planning Board under s.4, or the official department web page showing it. Also find the KTCP Rules that set its membership. If either is found, Part A = YES and the score would be 10/10. Also check the official law department or gazette text and any amendments after 2015 (the Act text here is a PRS republication, a secondary source).

question: Is there a provision for the establishment of Planning Authorities for notified new towns or special developments?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Yes. Karnataka's town planning law, the Karnataka Town and Country Planning (KTCP) Act, 1961, lets the State Government notify any area in the state as a Local Planning Area under s.4A(1). Once it has done so, s.4C(1) lets it set up a 'Planning Authority' for that area by gazette notification. The Act can also extend an existing planning area to cover an adjacent area. Every Planning Authority must then prepare a master plan for its area within two years of the area being declared (s.9(1)). The provision covers any newly notified area. The Act has no separate 'new town' or 'special development' authority clause. The power to set up an authority is discretionary ('may'), not a duty. | EVIDENCE: (1) KTCP Act 1961 (ULG-02, PRS text with amendments up to Act 38 of 2015), Chapter IA. s.4A(1): 'The State Government may by notification declare any area in the State to be a Local Planning Area for the purposes of this Act, or include within such local planning area, any area adjacent thereto'. s.4A(2): the notification must define the area's limits. s.4A(3): areas can be amalgamated or sub-divided after consulting the State Town-Planning Board. s.4C(1): 'As soon as may be, after declaration of a local planning area, the State Government in consultation with the Board, may, by notification in the official Gazette, constitute ... an authority to be called the "Planning Authority" of that area'. s.4C(2)-(3): the authority is a body corporate, with a Chairman and a Town Planning
quote: As soon as may be, after declaration of a local planning area, the State Government in consultation with the Board, may, by notification in the official Gazette, constitute for the purposes of the performance of the functions assigned to it, an authority to be called the “Planning Authority” of that area, having jurisdiction over that area.
chapter: Chapter IA – Local Planning Areas and Planning Authorities (inserted by Act 14 of 1964); Chapter III – Master Plan
provision: Section 4C(1) read with Section 4A(1) and Section 9(1)
clause: s.4A(1) (declare any area in the State to be a Local Planning Area, or include an adjacent area); s.4C(1) (constitute a Planning Authority for that area); s.9(1) (every planning authority shall prepare a master plan within two years of the area being declared)
comments: I checked the Step 2 answer against the text of ULG-02 and the source supports it. The source is the KTCP Act 1961, Karnataka Act 11 of 1963, in a PRS compilation with amendments up to Act 38 of 2015. Three provisions decide the answer. s.4A(1) says 'The State Government may by notification declare any area in the State to be a Local Planning Area for the purposes of this Act, or include within such local planning area, any area adjacent thereto'. s.4C(1) lets the State set up a 'Planning Authority' for that area by Gazette notification, as a body corporate with set membership (s.4C(2)-(3)). s.9(1), substituted by Act 1 of 2005, says 'Every planning authority shall ... not later than two years from the date of declaration of the local planning area, prepare and publish ... a master plan for such area'. Taken together, the Act provides for setting up a Planning Authority for any newly notified area. It also covers the methodology's other route: an adjacent area added to an existing planning area must be planned by that area's authority. On that basis the answer is YES. Points for a reviewer: (1) s.4C uses 'may', so setting up an authority is discretionary. The methodology only asks whether a provision exists, so this still counts as YES. (2) The Act has no clause naming 'new towns' or 'special developments'. The general power to notify a new Local Planning Area and set up its authority is what meets the test. (3) ULG-02 is a PRS compilation, a secondary source. Amendments after 2015 are not in the Citation Sheet. The 2025 KTCP Amendment Bill (ULG-03) is not shown to be enacted, so I did not rely on it. (4) The KTCP Rules and the Karnataka Urban Development Authorities Act 1987 are not in the Citation Sheet. They are not needed for a YES. Context only, not used for scoring: ULG-01 (GBA Act 2024) makes GBA the Planning Authority under the KTCP Act for the Greater Bengaluru Area, and ULG-04 (BDA Act s.67, which inserted KTCP s.81-B) does the same for BDA in the City of Bangalore.

question: Is there a provision for the establishment of Planning Authorities for notified new towns or special developments?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Very likely yes, but the provision itself cannot be read in the Citation Sheet. Three official sources say that the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 (GTPUD Act) lets the State constitute Area Development Authorities (s.5) and Urban Development Authorities (s.22) for areas declared as development areas. The development plan for such an area is prepared by that authority or by an officer the State authorises. However, the Citation Sheet copy of the Act (ULG-01, PRS) has no readable text for the principal Act (pages 2-86 are blank or scanned). So the actual wording of ss.3, 5 and 22 (the trigger, 'shall' or 'may', and whether new towns or special developments are covered) cannot be quoted or checked. | EVIDENCE: (1) Comprehensive General Development Control Regulations 2017 (CGDCR), Table 1.1, a binding state notification of the Urban Development and Urban Housing Department (ULG-14, p.1-2, and the same in ULG-05). It groups bodies as category D1 'Urban Development Authority (Constituted under Section 22 of The Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976)', which includes Surat Urban Development Authority (SUDA), and category D2 'Urban/ Area Development Authority (Constituted under Section 22 or 5...)'. Category D3 covers Area Development Authorities 'Constituted under Section 5' (e.g. Bhuj, Bhachau, Rapar, Anjar). (2) GTPUD Rules 1979 (ULG-04): r.3 has an 'authorized Officer' appointed under s.9(2) prepare the draft development plan 'withi
quote: D5(4) Area Development Authority (Constituted under Section 5 of The Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 (Special Project Areas) viz.:Alang Area Development Authority (AlADA)
chapter: 1 Preamble; 1.1 Short Title, Applicability & Commencement
provision: Regulation 1.1.3 Applicability, Table 1.1: Classification of Development Authorities, ULB's and other areas
clause: Categories D5 (Section 5 ADAs for Special Project Areas), D1/D2/D4 (Section 22 UDAs and Section 22 or 5 bodies), D3 (Section 5 ADAs)
comments:
Why YES: Under the methodology, the question is whether the state town planning law (here the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, the GTPUD Act) provides for setting up a planning authority for notified new areas or special developments. I checked the Step 2 answer against the sources and it holds up. The evidence is the CGDCR 2017 (ULG-14, the same text as ULG-05). This is a binding Gujarat UD&UHD notification made under GTPUD Act s.116A/122. Its Table 1.1 records the state government's statement of the legal basis for bodies that already exist. Category D5 is Area Development Authorities 'Constituted under Section 5' of the GTPUD Act for 'Special Project Areas' (Alang, Ambaji, Shamlaji, Khambhaliya). This fits 'special developments' directly. Other categories are D1, D2 and D4 (Urban Development Authorities under s.22, including SUDA), D3 (Section 5 Area Development Authorities in Seismic Zone V) and D7A/D7B (authorities designated under s.6). 

Other sources point the same way. (1) The GTPUD (Amendment) Act 2017, appended in ULG-01 (p.90), amends ss.7(2) and 23(2) so that the State 'may' delegate 'the powers and functions of the Area Development Authorities' and 'of the Urban Development Authorities' to local authorities. This shows that both kinds of authority are created by the Act. (2) GTPUD Rules 1979 (ULG-04) rr.3 and 5 refer to the 'area declared as development area' and the 'area development authority or ... the authorized officer'. So where no authority is constituted, an authorised officer prepares the plan, which also fits the methodology's alternative test. (3) SUDA's DP 2035 report (ULG-06, p.13) says the 1976 Act 'made the provision for formation of Urban / Area Development Authorities' for growth beyond municipal limits.

What to check (why confidence is low): The operative text of GTPUD Act ss.3, 5 and 22 cannot be read in ULG-01 (PRS copy; the principal Act's pages are scanned or blank). So I could not quote the exact trigger ('development area' or 'urban development area' declared by notification) or the verb ('may' or 'shall'). The YES rests on a binding state regulation and on amendment and Rules text that refer to these sections, not on the sections themselves. A reviewer should get readable official text of ss.3, 5 and 22 to confirm. Also confirm that UPD2 scores YES = 10 and NO = 0; the methodology does not state bands. I did not check the Gujarat Special Investment Region Act or the GIDC Act 1962 because they are not in the Citation Sheet. They are not needed for YES, since the GTPUD Act provision is enough.

question: Does the Act require three levels of spatial plans for cities: Metropolitan/Regional, Municipal and Ward(s) /Local >:< Metropolitan/ Regional Plan
step2_answer: ANSWER: Yes. Karnataka law requires a metropolitan plan for Bengaluru. Clause (2)(c) of the Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 uses 'shall' twice. The State Government must set up a Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Committee (BMPC), with membership as laid down in Article 243ZE of the Constitution, for an area at least as large as the Greater Bengaluru Area. A named planning body must then prepare a draft development plan for the Greater Bengaluru Area as a whole. On the regional side, the official BMRDA website lists preparing a structure plan for the Bangalore Metropolitan Region as one of the functions the Authority 'shall' have. Who prepares what: the metropolitan draft development plan is assigned to the 'Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Authority' (this is the Act's wording, inside the BMPC clause). The Chief Commissioner of the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) is the BMPC's Member Secretary, and the Chief Minister chairs it. BMRDA, a state body, prepares the regional structure plan. Separately, the GBA is the KTCP 'Planning Authority' for the Greater Bengaluru Area and must make its master plan. | EVIDENCE: (1) ULG-01, Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024, chapter on GBA functions, sub-section (2) 'Planning Functions', clause (c) (the section number is probably 14; this is only a location note): 'The State Government shall constitute the Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Committee (BMPC)... The Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Authority shall prepare a draft developm
quote: The Chief Commissioner of the Greater Bengaluru Authority shall be its Member Secretary. The Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Authority shall prepare a draft development plan for the Greater Bengaluru Area as a whole
chapter: Chapter III – Greater Bengaluru Authority (section on the GBA's functions)
provision: Section on the functions of the Greater Bengaluru Authority, sub-section (2) 'Planning Functions' (the section number is probably 14, but the excerpt does not confirm it)
comments:
Scored YES. Bengaluru is a metropolitan city. In the Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 (Karnataka Act 36 of 2025), the 'Planning Functions' sub-section, clause (2)(c), says the State Government 'shall constitute' the Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Committee (BMPC). The BMPC covers an area 'including but not limited to the Greater Bengaluru Area', and its membership follows Article 243ZE. The same clause says a draft development plan for the Greater Bengaluru Area as a whole 'shall' be prepared. Both duties use 'shall', so this is a binding requirement for a metropolitan plan, not a 'may'. The methodology lets us count a metropolitan authority Act as evidence. Section 103(1)(b) of the same Act backs this up: Ward Development Plans must be drawn up 'in accordance with the plans prepared by the Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Committee'.

On the regional side, the official BMRDA Functions page (ULG-10) says the Authority's functions 'shall be' to 'prepare a structure plan' for the Bangalore Metropolitan Region. This is only the website's restatement of the BMRDA Act, 1985. The Act's own text is not in the Citation Sheet, so it is supporting evidence only.

I checked the source against the Step 2 answer and it supports it. The YES rests on the GBA Act provision.

Caveats for the reviewer:
(1) Drafting mismatch: the clause sets up the 'BMPC' but gives the plan-preparing duty to the 'Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Authority', a body the excerpt never creates. The duty is mandatory either way. A reviewer should check the official Gazette text, because ULG-01 is a PRS copy.
(2) The mandated plan covers the Greater Bengaluru Area 'as a whole', not the wider BMRDA region.
(3) I could not confirm the commencement date or the GBA era from the Sheet.
(4) ULG-02 (KTCP Act) was not fully searched for a regional-plan chapter. This does not affect a YES that already rests on a binding provision.

I scored only the Metropolitan/Regional sub-question (SQ, max 3.33).

Clause 9 adds new s.10A to the MPC Act: "The State Government may, on receipt of the draft development plan submitted by the Metropolitan Planning Committee... either (a) sanction or refuse to sanction... or (b) return the draft development plan to the metropolitan planning committee". s.10A(3): the final development plan "shall be binding on the concerned all authorities functioning in the metropolitan area". s.10C(3)(a): an officer appointed by the State shall "assist the metropolitan planning committee in the preparation of the development plan under the Act". These sections deal with sanctioning and assisting the plan. They do n

comments:
The Answer is left blank because the Citation Sheet does not show whether a metropolitan plan is mandatory. A 'NO' would need affirmative absence, and that is not possible here.

What the sources show: Gujarat law does provide for a metropolitan-level development plan. The 2019 amending Act (Guj. 14 of 2019) is appended to the PRS copy of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 (TPUD Act) in ULG-01. It inserts the following into the Gujarat Metropolitan Planning Committees Act, 2008 (MPC Act):

- s.10A(3): the final plan 'shall be binding on the concerned all authorities functioning in the metropolitan area'.
- s.10C(3)(a): a State-appointed officer shall assist the Committee 'in the preparation of the development plan under the Act'.

The same Act also amends the TPUD Act. It adds a proviso to s.9(1) and a new s.19A, which say the local development plan 'shall include' the spatial proposals of the sanctioned MPC plan.

These provisions only cover sanctioning (and s.10A(1) uses 'may'), the plan's binding effect, and help with preparing it. They assume a metropolitan plan will exist. None of them is itself a 'shall prepare' duty.

The provision that would decide this question is not in the Citation Sheet: the MPC Act, 2008's own section requiring the Committee to prepare a draft development plan for the metropolitan area.

- ULG-03: the GPMC Act, 1949. It covers re-development plans only.
- ULG-04: the TPUD Rules, 1979. They cover the authority's development plan, not a metropolitan or regional plan.
- ULG-05/14/15/16: the CGDCR 2017.
- ULG-06: SUDA DP 2035. This is context only. It says the Surat Metropolitan area was declared under the MPC Act on 11/03/2016, and that as of 2017 the MPC development plan was 'not in place'.
- ULG-09: the NITI Aayog plan, which is non-statutory.
- Searches for 'regional plan' and 'Metropolitan Planning Committee shall prepare draft development plan' found no mandate.

Other caveats:
- The 2019 Act comes into force on a date the State notifies, and no commencement notification is in the sheet.
- ULG-01 is a secondary PRS republication.

ACTION: The research team should add the official text of the Gujarat MPC Act, 2008 (Guj. 18 of 2008) and check whether it says the MPC 'shall' prepare a draft development plan for the metropolitan area. question: Does the Act require three levels of spatial plans for cities: Metropolitan/Regional, Municipal and Ward(s) /Local >:< Municipal/city plan
step2_answer: ANSWER: Yes. Section 9(1) of the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961 says every planning authority 'shall' prepare and publish a master plan for its area. This is the city-level spatial plan. The deadline is two years from the date the local planning area is declared, and the plan goes to the State Government, through the Director, for provisional approval. If the authority misses the deadline, s.9(2) lets the State authorise the Director to prepare the plan and recover the cost from the authority. So the plan is required whoever the planning authority is. For Bengaluru, the Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 names the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) as that planning authority for the Greater Bengaluru Area. Before that, KTCP s.81-B and BDA Act s.67 named the Bangalore Development Authority (BDA). The State approves the plan; the city body prepares it. | EVIDENCE: (1) KTCP Act (PRS compilation, amended up to Act 38 of 2015). s.2(3-b), inserted by Act 1 of 2005, defines a master plan as 'a plan for the development or re-development of the area within the jurisdiction of a planning authority'. s.9(1), substituted w.e.f. 14.2.2005: 'Every planning authority shall, as soon as may be, carry out a survey ... and shall, not later than two years from the date of declaration of the local planning area, prepare and publish ... a master plan'. s.9(2) is the Director fallback. s.10(1): the planning authority 'shall' declare its intention to prepare the plan and invite pub
quote: Every planning authority shall, as soon as may be, carry out a survey of the area within its jurisdiction and shall, not later than two years from the date of declaration of the local planning area, prepare and publish in the prescribed manner a master plan for such area and submit it to the State Government, through the Director, for provisional approval.
chapter: Chapter III (heading 'Outline Development Plan' in the compilation, changed to 'Master Plan' by Act 1 of 2005)
provision: Section 9(1), Preparation of Master Plan (substituted by Act 1 of 2005 w.e.f. 14.2.2005)
clause: s.9(1); read with s.2(3-b) (definition of master plan), s.9(2) (Director fallback), s.10(1), s.12 and s.13-B
comments:
UPD3b asks whether the state planning law requires a municipal/city plan. The answer is YES. Section 9(1) of the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961 (PRS compilation, amended up to Act 38 of 2015; s.9 is in its 2005 substituted form) says every planning authority 'shall' prepare and publish a master plan for its area within two years of the local planning area being declared. Section 2(3-b), inserted by Act 1 of 2005, defines a master plan as 'a plan for the development or re-development of the area within the jurisdiction of a planning authority'. That is the city-level spatial plan.

Other provisions back this up:
- s.9(2): if the planning authority misses the deadline, the State may authorise the Director to prepare the plan and recover the cost from the authority.
- s.10(1): the authority 'shall' declare its intention to prepare the plan.
- s.12: 'The Master Plan shall consist of' set contents, such as land-use zoning and the street pattern.
- s.13-B: a master plan is also required for any area added to the authority's jurisdiction.

So the plan is mandatory ('shall'), not discretionary ('may'). Revision under s.13-D is discretionary unless the State directs it, but that does not affect whether a city plan must exist.

Applying this to Bengaluru: KTCP s.81-B (inserted by BDA Act s.67) names the Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) as the planning authority. The Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 (ULG-01, 'Planning Functions' provision) makes the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) the 'Planning Authority' under KTCP for the Greater Bengaluru Area. I checked this against the Step 2 answer and the source text; I did not re-read ULG-01 here. The State approves the plan, but the planning authority must prepare it.

What a person should check:
- When the GBA designation took effect, and whether the KTCP Amendment Bill 2025 (ULG-03) was enacted. Neither changes the answer, because s.9 binds whichever body is the planning authority.
- The text relied on is a PRS compilation, not the Gazette copy.
- The planning authority (BDA, now GBA) is a development or metropolitan authority, not the municipal council itself. The methodology lets a development authority Act count as evidence, so this should not matter.

One point for scoring: the sheet gives a max of 3.33 but no rubric bands, so YES is treated as full marks for this sub-question (3 x 3.33 for UPD3). The metropolitan and ward levels belong to UPD3a and UPD3c and are not assessed here.

question: Is there a clear decentralised procedure for approvals of each level of plans? >:< Does the law mandate that the metropolitan/regional plan be approved by the state government?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Probably yes, but this is not confirmed. The amended Gujarat Metropolitan Planning Committees Act, 2008 (MPC Act) makes the State Government the only body that can sanction the metropolitan development plan. It can sanction it, refuse it or send it back for changes. The plan becomes the 'final development plan', binding on all authorities in the metropolitan area, only once the State sanctions it. However, the operative verb is 'may', not 'shall'. Also, nothing in the Citation Sheet shows that the 2019 amendment inserting this provision has come into force. | EVIDENCE: (1) MPC Act s.10A, inserted by clause 9 of the Gujarat Local Authorities and Town Planning Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 (Gazette Ex. 19-08-2019, PRS copy ULG-01 p.97). s.10A(1): '(a) sanction or refuse to sanction the draft development plan ... or (b) return the draft development plan to the metropolitan planning committee or the authorized officer ... for modifying the plan as it may direct'. s.10A(2): 'The sanction accorded under clause (a) of sub section (1), shall be called the final development plan', which comes into force on the date the State notifies. s.10A(3): binding on 'all authorities functioning in the metropolitan area'. The opening words of MPC s.10A(1) are cut off in both copies. Answer: YES, with low confidence and points for a person to check.

(1) The metropolitan plan. MPC Act s.10A(1), inserted by Gujarat Act 14 of 2019, says: 'The State Government may, on receipt of the draft development plan submitted by the Metropolitan Planning Committee, by notification in the Official Gazette, either' (a) sanction or refuse to sanction it, or (b) return it for changes. The OCR of this opening line in ULG-01 p.97 is garbled but readable. Under s.10A(2), only the plan the State sanctions becomes the 'final development plan', and it comes into force on a date the State notifies. Under s.10A(3), only that plan binds all authorities in the metropolitan area. Variations also need State sanction (s.10B), and the State's decision on disputes is final (s.10C(2)). The word 'may' sets the State's choice of outcome: sanction, refuse or return. It does not make State approval optional. No other body can sanction the plan, and no plan becomes final without the State. So I read this as State approval being required by law. A person should confirm this reading of 'may'.

(2) A second route via the development authority plan (GTPUD Act). If Surat's regional plan is taken to be the SUDA development plan, State approval is again required:
- GTPUD Rules 1979 r.3 (ULG-04): the officer 'shall submit the same to the State Government through the Chief Town Planner'.

(3) Points to check:
- (a) s.1(2) of the 2019 amending Act says it comes into force on a date the State notifies. No commencement notification is in the Citation Sheet, so it is not proven that MPC s.10A is in force. The GTPUD route in point 2 does not depend on this.

question: Does the law mandate participation of all parastatals/ agencies /ULGs in creation of Spatial plans (metro/municipal/ward)?

The GBA Act says the GBA shall be the 'Planning Authority' under the KTCP Act, and that its members shall include the Mayors of the City Corporations and the heads of BDA, BWSSB, BMTC, BMRCL and BESCOM. At metropolitan level, the GBA Act says the State shall set up a Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Committee (BMPC) whose make-up follows Art. 243ZE. The Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961 (KTCP Act) requires the Planning Authority to ask the public for suggestions when it declares it will prepare a Master Plan, and later to publish the plan inviting public comments, which it 'shall consider'. The Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 (GBG Act) makes the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) the Planning Authority for the Greater Bengaluru Area, so these duties fall on GBA. Part A (ward committees / Area Sabhas) is NOT FOUND, but not confirmed absent. In the KTCP Act text I read, ward committees, Ward Sabhas and Area Sabhas take no part in preparing the Master Plan. The only participation duty through a Ward Sabha in Bengaluru's law is in the GBG Act, and it covers the annual Ward Development Plan, not the city Master Plan. Other layers were not read, so a 0 for Part A cannot be justified yet. | EVIDENCE: (1) KTCP Act s.10(1), as substituted by Act 1 of 2005: the Planning Authority 'shall publish a notice of such declaration in the Official Gazette and also in one or more local newspaper in the prescribed manner calling suggestions from the public within a period of sixty days'. (2) KTCP Act s.13(1): the plan is returned to the Planning Authority, 'which shall thereupon publish, by notification, the plan and the reports inviting public comments within sixty days'. s.13(2): if a member of the public sends comments, 'the Planning authority shall consider such comments and resubmit

comments:
SCORE: Part B can be filled. Part A stays blank, so the total score is open. It would be 5 if Part A is confirmed NO, or 10 if YES.

PART B = YES. The Karnataka Town and Country Planning (KTCP) Act has two mandatory public-input steps for the Master Plan:
- s.10(1): the Planning Authority 'shall publish a notice' 'calling suggestions from the public within a period of sixty days'. s.10(2): the Planning Authority 'shall consider such suggestion'.
- s.13(1): the Planning Authority 'shall thereupon publish, by notification, the plan and the reports inviting public comments within sixty days'. s.13(2): it 'shall consider such comments' and resubmit with recommended changes.
Both use 'shall', and both are open to every member of the public. The methodology credits these under Part B even though no specific method is required.

WHO THE DUTIES FALL ON:
- Greater Bengaluru Governance (GBG) Act (ULG-01), Planning Functions sub-section (2)(a): the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) 'shall be the "Planning Authority" as defined under the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961'.
- The 2025 KTCP Amendment Bill (ULG-03) would add a new s.81-G with the same effect. It is still a Bill: it comes into force only on a date the State notifies, and it says nothing about participation.

PART A = BLANK. This is 'not found', not proven absent. What I checked:
- KTCP Act s.6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13 and 13-A (ULG-02): none mentions ward committees, Ward Sabhas or Area Sabhas in preparing the Master Plan.
- The 2020 Second Amendment (Act 47 of 2020, appended in ULG-02):
  - It requires ward-level land-use maps and their display 'in the offices of the local authorities and the ward offices'.
  - It adds to s.13(1) that the plan 'shall be forwarded to the local authorities within the local planning area'.
  - That is display at offices and forwarding to the local authority, not a ward committee or Area Sabha process.
  - However, the rest of the s.13(1) insertion is cut off in the saved text, so I could not confirm all of its wording.
- GBG Act (ULG-01):
  - s.103(1)(b)-(c): the Ward Sabha's role covers only the annual Ward Development Plan, which is a budget priority list. That is not the city Master Plan.
  - The clause on the Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Committee's draft development plan (Planning Functions (2)(c)) is cut off at 'and disc...', so I could not read whether it requires consulting ward committees.
- ULG-03 (2025 Bill): it deals only with the Commissionerate and the Planning Authority's jurisdiction. It has no participation provisions.
- The KTCP Rules, which set the 'prescribed manner' for these notices, are not in the Citation Sheet.

The 0 for Part A cannot be given until a reviewer checks three things: the full s.13(1) text from the 2020 amendment, the full GBG Act Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Committee clause, and the KTCP Rules.

question: Does the law mandate public participation in preparation of the municipal plan through Area Sabhas / Ward Sabhas and other means?

Under the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 (GTPUD Act), as carried out by Rule 5 of the 1979 Rules, the draft development plan must be published, and objections and suggestions from any member of the public must be invited within two months and considered. For Surat, Surat Urban Development Authority (SUDA) prepares this plan, and its area includes the Surat Municipal Corporation (SMC) area. Part A (ward committees or area sabhas) is not determined. The sheet has no provision requiring ward committees or area sabhas to take part in preparing the plan. chapter: Chapter II
provision: Rule 5 (Manner of publication of draft development plan and form of notice for inviting suggestions or modifications to the draft development plan under section 13); also Rule 6 and Form A
clause: r.5(1)-(2); r.6(1)-(2) (as amended by Notification dated 22-01-87); Form A (citing s.13(1))
comments: PART B = YES. I checked the Step 2 answer against the source. Under ULG-04, the GTPUD Rules 1979 (made under the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976): r.5(1) says the authority 'shall' publish the draft development plan in the Official Gazette and in Gujarati newspapers. r.5(2) says the notice 'shall', 'in pursuance of the provisions of section 13', invite written objections or suggestions from any member of the public within two months. The authority 'shall consider' them. Only modifying the plan is discretionary ('may modify'). Form A is issued 'in pursuance of sub-section (1) of section 13 of the said Act' and says objections and suggestions 'from any person … shall be considered'. Under r.6(1) and (2), substantial modifications made by the authority or by the State are republished for public objections, which 'shall be considered' before sanction. This fits the methodology's footnote: a provision for consolidating suggestions and objections counts as 'other means'. The Act's own s.13 text cannot be read in ULG-01: the PRS copy's pages 2-86 are scanned with no text layer. So the YES rests on the Rules, which state they implement the mandate in s.13. The reviewer should confirm that the Rules are enough to show the Act 'mandates' this. That is why confidence is medium-to-low. This is a general notice to the public, not ward-level consultation. PART A = blank (not found; absence not proven). I found no provision requiring ward committees or area sabhas to take part in preparing the development plan in: GTPUD Rules r.3, r.5 and r.6; the readable GTPUD amendment Acts (6 of 2017, 22 of 2017, 14 of 2019 in ULG-01 and Bill 21 of 2019 in ULG-02); the 2019 amendments to the MPC and DPC Acts (ss.10A-10C, which provide only 'any person' objections to variations); and GPMC Act s.29A (ULG-03, Wards Committees, whose functions are left to State rules under s.29A(8)). A search across the whole Citation Sheet for 'ward committee area sabha development plan participation' returned nothing relevant. But I cannot record affirmative absence. The main text of the GTPUD Act, including ss.9-17, is unreadable. The Wards Committee rules under GPMC s.29A(8) are not in the sheet. The full text of the Gujarat Metropolitan Planning Committees Act, 2008 is not in the sheet. A human should check these three instruments. question: Is there public scrutiny for (including objections and responses) municipal/city plan? >:< Does the law mandate public scrutiny for (including objections and responses) municipal/city plan through Area Sabhas / Ward Sabhas and other means?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Part B (other means) is met. The Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act (KTCP Act) requires the Master Plan to be published for public comment, and the Planning Authority must consider those comments and send the plan back with recommended changes. Part A (Ward Committees / Area Sabhas) is NOT FOUND for the city plan. The Act sections read do not mention ward committees, ward sabhas or area sabhas. The city's own law, the Greater Bengaluru Governance Act (GBA Act), uses a Ward Sabha only for the Annual Ward Development Plan, not for the Master Plan. I could not show the absence for every layer, because the KTCP Rules are not in the Citation Sheet and one GBA Act planning clause could not be read in full. So Part A is undetermined, not 0. | EVIDENCE: (1) KTCP Act s.13(1), as substituted by Act 1 of 2005: after provisional approval, the Planning Authority 'shall thereupon publish, by notification, the plan and the reports inviting public comments within sixty days of such publication'. (2) s.13(2): 'the Planning authority shall consider such comments and resubmit the plan and the reports to the State Government ... with recommendations for such modifications'. This is a mandatory scrutiny, objection and response step for the city plan, so it meets Part B. (3) s.13(3)-(4): the State Government gives final approval 'in the light of the comments'. The approved plan is published and kept open for public inspection. (4) s.13-A(1): the s.13 procedure also applies to Interim
quote: If within sixty days of the publication under sub-section (1), any member of the public communicates in writing to the Planning Authority any comments on the plan and the reports, the Planning authority shall consider such comments and resubmit the plan and the reports to the State Government, through the Director with recommendations for such modifications in the plan and reports as it considers necessary in the light of the public comments made on the plan and reports.
chapter: Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961 (Karnataka Act 11 of 1963), Chapter on Master Plans; PRS compilation with amendments up to Act 38 of 2015
provision: Section 13 (Approval of the Master Plan), as substituted by Act 1 of 2005 with effect from 14.2.2005; see also s.10(1)-(2) and s.13-A(1)
comments:
PART B = YES. The KTCP Act requires the Planning Authority to publicise the Master Plan and to answer what the public says. Under s.13(1), the plan returned by the State Government 'shall thereupon publish, by notification, the plan and the reports inviting public comments within sixty days'. Under s.13(2), the Planning Authority 'shall consider such comments and resubmit' the plan with recommended changes 'in the light of the public comments'. Section 10(1)-(2) adds a mandatory earlier step: the declaration of intention is published 'calling suggestions from the public within a period of sixty days', and the Planning Authority 'shall consider such suggestion'. Under s.13-A(1), the s.13 procedure also applies to Interim Master Plans. All of these are 'shall' duties covering scrutiny, comments and the response, so Part B is met (2.5). For Bengaluru, GBA Act s.14(2)(a) (ULG-01) makes the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) the 'Planning Authority' under the KTCP Act for the Greater Bengaluru Area. ULG-03, a 2025 amendment Bill (inserting s.81-G), says the same, but it is the Bill as passed by the Assembly and I have not confirmed it is in force.

PART A = BLANK (not found; affirmative absence not shown). What I checked: (1) KTCP Act ss.9, 10, 12, 13 and 13-A (ULG-02). No ward committee, ward sabha or area sabha appears in the Master Plan procedure. (2) ULG-03, the KTCP Amendment Bill 2025. It covers the Commissionerate and the GBA as Planning Authority. It has no participation provisions. (3) BDA Act ss.17-18 (ULG-04). These cover development schemes, with representations from 'the Corporation' and notices to affected owners. That is not ward-level scrutiny of the Master Plan, and since the GBA was set up the BDA is no longer the Planning Authority for the Greater Bengaluru Area. (4) GBA Act s.103(1)(b)-(c) (ULG-01). The Ward Sabha meets only 'for providing inputs for the formulation of the Annual Ward Development Plan', which is a budget priority list. It is not scrutiny of the Master Plan. Section 103(1)(d) lets the Ward Committee call general meetings on any issue, but that is a general power, not a requirement to scrutinise the city plan. I did not use the BBMP Act 2020 (ULG-19), which had Area Sabhas: it is a BBMP-era law that the GBA Act replaced.

Why Part A is blank and not NO: (a) The GBA Act clause on the Bengaluru Metropolitan Planning Committee's draft development plan (s.14(2)(c)) is cut off at 'shall prepare a draft development plan ... and disc...' in every excerpt I could get, so I could not check it for a ward-level consultation step. (b) The KTCP Rules, which set the 'prescribed manner' of publication under ss.9, 10 and 13(4), are not in the Citation Sheet. A reviewer should read the full s.14(2)(c) and the KTCP Rules. If neither requires ward committee or area sabha scrutiny, Part A = NO (0) and the total = 2.5/5. If either does, Part A = YES and the total = 5/5.

Other notes: The Step 2 answer is consistent with the source. The KTCP text I used goes only to 2015 (PRS compilation, a secondary source), and later amendments are not in the Citation Sheet.

Any member of the public may send written objections or suggestions within two months, and the authority 'shall consider' them. Rule 6 adds a second round of notice and objections when the draft is changed substantially, first by the planning authority and then by the State Government. Part A (Ward Committees / Area Sabhas): not found. The Rules give only gazette, newspaper and posted notices. But the main sections of the Town Planning Act, the Ward Committees' functions under the Municipal Corporations Act, and any Area Sabha law were not all available or read, so I cannot treat this as a confirmed absence. The Surat Municipal Corporation (SMC) prepares Town Planning Schemes. | EVIDENCE: (1) Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Rules, 1979 (ULG-04): r.5(1): the authority 'shall... cause the development plan also published by means of a notice in the Official Gazette, and in one or more Gujarati newspaper

comments: PART B = YES (worth 2.50). The Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Rules, 1979 (ULG-04) set out a public scrutiny process for the draft development plan under GTPUD Act s.13. Under r.5(1), the plan 'shall' be published by notice in the Official Gazette and in Gujarati newspapers, and copies are pasted at the head office and at prominent places. Under r.5(2), any member of the public may send objections or suggestions in writing within two months, and the authority 'shall consider' them. This is a binding rule ('shall'), so it meets Part B ('other means', including scrutiny or objections where no mode is specified). step2_answer: ANSWER: Yes. Surat's city plan is the Development Plan 2035 of the Surat Urban Development Authority (SUDA). The State Government then told SUDA to submit the plan together with the suggestions and objections received. Under s.14, SUDA 'has to submit the Draft Development Plan - 2035 to the State Government along with opinion on such objections and suggestions'. Ch.21, p.217: by letter dated 21.11.2016, UD&UHD told SUDA to submit the draft 'along with the sugge stions and objections received for the proposals on the Draft Development plan - 2035 published u/s 13'. comments:
This sub-question asks about implementation: was public scrutiny actually carried out? The methodology says to score 5 if there is evidence of public scrutiny in the Development Authority's or ULG's material, including the plan itself. I checked the Step 2 answer against ULG-06 (SUDA Development Plan 2035 report, dated 22 Feb 2017), and the report supports it.

What the report shows:
(1) The draft DP 2035 was published in the Official Gazette under s.13 on 10 May 2016. A notice in a Gujarati daily on 11 May 2016 invited suggestions and objections from the public within two months (p.216).
(2) Under s.14, SUDA had to submit the draft to the State Government together with its opinion on those objections and suggestions (p.216).
(3) In a letter dated 21.11.2016, UD&UHD told SUDA to submit the draft 'along with the suggestions and objections received for the proposals on the Draft Development plan - 2035 published u/s 13' (p.217). This shows objections were actually received, not just invited.

(b) For the 'responses' part, the evidence is only the s.14 duty to give an opinion on objections and the state's direction to forward the objections received. The Citation Sheet has no itemised register of objections with a response to each.

question: Does the law mandate periodic review and revision of the notified municipal/city plan, including corresponding revisions to the Development Control Regulations (DCRs)?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Only in part. Section 13-D of the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act (KTCP Act) gives a revision timeline ('at least once in every ten years') and names the body responsible (the Planning Authority, or the State Government by direction). Revision is not mandatory, though: the Planning Authority 'may' revise, and 'shall' only 'if directed so by the State Government'. When a revision does happen, sections 9 to 12 apply to it. Section 12 makes Zoning Regulations, zone-wise regulations and building-line, height and FAR controls part of the Master Plan, so a revised plan has to carry revised development regulations. Under the Greater Bengaluru Governance Act (GBG Act), the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) is the Planning Authority for the Greater Bengaluru Area. | EVIDENCE: (1) KTCP Act s.13-D 'Revision of Master Plan' (inserted by Amendment Act 2004; PRS compilation p.34-35 and p.119): 'At least once in every ten years ... the Planning Authority may and if directed so by the State Government shall, carryout a fresh survey ... with a view to revising the existing Master Plan and the provisions of section 9 to section 12 (both inclusive) shall mutatis mutandis apply in respect of such revision'. (2) KTCP Act s.12(1)(a): the Master Plan 'shall include proposals for ... zoning of land use ... together with Zoning Regulations'. s.12(1)(f): areas of special control subject to regulations on 'building line, height of the building, floor area ratio'. s.12(2)(iii): 'regulati
quote: At least once in every ten years from the date on which the Master Plan has come into force, subject to the provisions of section 13-C, the Planning Authority may and if directed so by the State Government shall, carryout a fresh survey of the area within its jurisdiction, with a view to revising the existing Master Plan and the provisions of  section 9 to section 12 (both inclusive) shall mutatis mutandis apply in respect of such revision of the Master Plan.
chapter: Chapter III (Master Plan)
provision: Section 13-D (Revision of Master Plan), read with Section 12(1)(a), 12(1)(f) and 12(2)(iii)
clause: s.13-D; s.12(1)(a) 'together with Zoning Regulations'; s.12(2)(iii) 'regulations in respect of each land use zone'
comments:
The inputs add up to 7.5 of 10 (C2 + C3 + C4 at 2.5 each). I checked the Step 2 answer against the source text, and it holds.

C1, periodic review mandated = NO: This NO rests on a provision I found and read, not on a gap in the evidence. Under KTCP Act s.13-D the Planning Authority 'may' revise the plan. It 'shall' revise only 'if directed so by the State Government'. The law therefore allows periodic revision but does not require it. The methodology also says that ten-year wording about revision should not count for C1. Other provisions I checked do not create a periodic duty either:
- s.13-B proviso: 'shall revise', but only when an additional area is added or the State directs. That is triggered by an event, not periodic.
- s.13-E: the State Government 'may' amend regulations. Discretionary.
- GBG Act 2024 (ULG-01), Planning Functions sub-section (2)(a): makes the GBA the Planning Authority under the KTCP Act. Its s.315(l) only lets the GBA make regulations on Master Plan contents. Neither sets up a revision cycle.
- 2025 KTCP Amendment Bill (ULG-03): inserts s.81-G and amends s.2(7) and s.81-B. It does not touch s.13-D.
The KTCP Rules are not in the Citation Sheet, so I could not check them. The methodology points to the State Town Planning Act.

C2, timeline = YES: s.13-D says 'At least once in every ten years from the date on which the Master Plan has come into force'.

C3, responsible authority = YES: s.13-D names the 'Planning Authority', with the State Government able to direct it. Under GBG Act Planning Functions (2)(a), the GBA is the Planning Authority for the Greater Bengaluru Area. ULG-03 would make this explicit through s.81-G, but there is no evidence it has been enacted.

C4, matching DCR revision = YES, by reading two sections together: s.13-D says ss.9 to 12 'shall mutatis mutandis apply' to a revision. Under s.12(1)(a) the Master Plan 'shall include proposals for ... zoning of land use ... together with Zoning Regulations'. Under s.12(1)(f) it covers regulations on building line, height and FAR. Under s.12(2)(iii), 'regulations in respect of each land use zone to enforce the provisions of such plan' must be published with the plan. A revised plan must therefore come with revised zoning regulations.

For the reviewer to check:
(a) Whether the s.12 Zoning Regulations count as 'DCRs' under the rubric. The Act never uses the words 'Development Control Regulations'. If they do not count, the score drops to 5.
(b) Whether C2 and C3 can be credited even though revision is not mandatory (C1 not met).
(c) Whether s.13-D was amended after the PRS compilation (amendments up to Act 38 of 2015). The PRS copy is a secondary source, so an official consolidated text should be checked.

question: Does the law mandate periodic review and revision of the notified municipal/city plan, including corresponding revisions to the Development Control Regulations (DCRs)?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Not established from the Act's own text. The only source in the Citation Sheet that addresses this is SUDA's Development Plan 2035 report. It says section 21 of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 (GTPUD Act) requires the development plan to be revised once in 10 years. This would suggest a fixed revision timeline, with the area development authority (here the Surat Urban Development Authority, SUDA) preparing the revision and the State Government sanctioning it. I could not read section 21 itself, so I cannot confirm its wording ('shall' or 'may'), the responsible authority, or whether it also requires the regulations (DCRs) to be revised. I found no source in the Sheet that requires the DCRs to be revised after a plan revision. | EVIDENCE: (1) ULG-06, SUDA Development Plan 2035 report (22-02-2017), p.40 (also p.30): 'As per the provisions of section 21 of the Act, the development plan is to be revised once in 10 years'. It records the plan history: first plan in force 1986, revised plan in force 15-09-2004, then DP-2035. This is a planning body describing the law, not the statute. (2) ULG-01, GTPUD Act 1976 (PRS copy with amendments): the passages I could retrieve were only the 2017 and 2019 amending Acts. The 2019 Act inserted s.19A: the appropriate authority 'shall include' the spatial proposals of District/Metropolitan Planning Committee plans 'by varying the development plan under section 19'. The text of s.21 did not come up in any search.

comments:
I left all four inputs blank. The deciding provision, s.21 of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act 1976 (GTPUD Act), cannot be read anywhere in the Citation Sheet.

(1) ULG-01 (PRS copy of the GTPUD Act): I read it from the start. The principal Act is on pages 2-86, and those pages are a scan with no readable text; they came back empty. Section 12(2) lists the reports to be sent with the plan, and section 12(3) covers heritage buildings and precincts. None of these mentions disaster, hazard, flood or resilience. That amendment only bars allotting land near storm water drains, tank beds and similar areas. That is a land-allotment limit, not a planning mandate.

(2) The only mandatory provision found is in an allied Act. Section 270(3) of the Greater Bengaluru Governance (GBA) Act, 2024 says the City Corporation 'shall prepare a Disaster Management Plan or Fire Hazard Response and Mitigation Plan every year'. I did not mark this YES, for three reasons:

question: Does the T&CP Act mandate the planning for:   >:< c) Comprehensive mobility
step2_answer: ANSWER: Yes. Karnataka law makes mobility planning mandatory for Bengaluru through two instruments. (1) Under the Bengaluru Metropolitan Land Transport Authority (BMLTA) Act, 2022 (the allied Act), the BMLTA 'shall' prepare a Comprehensive Mobility Plan (CMP) for the Urban Mobility Region. The Act sets a time limit and what the plan must contain, and requires a revision at least every five years. Section 22 then says the Planning Authority 'shall' prepare the land use plan in its Master Plan taking the CMP into account 'in its entirety'. The Planning Authority must also consult the BMLTA, and the BMLTA must concur in the draft Master Plan. (2) Under the Karnataka Town and Country Planning (KTCP) Act, 1961, the Master Plan that every Planning Authority 'shall' prepare (s.9(1)) 'shall include' a complete street pattern and a traffic circulation pattern (s.12(1)(b)). That is a mandatory mobility part of the city plan. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) is the KTCP 'Planning Authority' for the Greater Bengaluru Area. So the city government's Master Plan must carry a mobility component and must line up with the CMP. The CMP itself is prepared by the BMLTA (a state body) and approved by the State Government. | EVIDENCE: BMLTA Act (ULG-18): s.21(1) 'The Authority shall notify its intent to prepare a Comprehensive Mobility Plan'; s.21(2) 'shall cause to prepare a Comprehensive Mobility Plan for the Urban Mobility Region within two years', listing required contents (a)-(m) such as
quote: The Planning Authority  in  the  Urban Mobility Region shall prepare the land use plan as part of preparation or revision of Master Plan of the city or local planning area by taking into consideration the Comprehensive Mobility Plan in its entirety.
chapter: Chapter V – Preparation of policies and Comprehensive Mobility Plan
provision: Sections 21, 22 and 23
comments: The answer is YES because Karnataka law requires mobility planning to be done with 'shall', not 'may'. I checked the Step 2 answer against the source text and it holds. (1) Allied Act (ULG-18, the BMLTA Act 2022, Karnataka Act 6 of 2023). Section 21(1) says 'The Authority shall notify its intent to prepare a Comprehensive Mobility Plan'. Section 21(2) says it 'shall cause to prepare a Comprehensive Mobility Plan for the Urban Mobility Region' within two years, and lists what the plan must contain in items (a)-(m): road network, road hierarchy, public transport routes, footpaths and cycle tracks, and accessible mobility. Section 23 requires a revision 'at least once in every five years' ('shall'). Section 22(1) requires the Planning Authority to prepare the land-use part of the Master Plan taking the CMP 'in its entirety' ('shall'). Section 22(2)-(3) requires it to consult the BMLTA and send it the draft Master Plan for concurrence. (2) The KTCP Act itself (ULG-02, s.12(1), as substituted by Act 1 of 2005) says the Master Plan 'shall include proposals for ... (b) a complete street pattern ... and traffic circulation pattern, for meeting immediate and future requirements with proposals for improvements'. That is a required mobility part of the city plan. Either route meets the methodology: a required CMP, or a required mobility component in the municipal/city plan. Provisions I did not rely on because they say 'may': s.21(6) (review whenever necessary) and the proviso to s.23 (revising the plan alongside the Master Plan). Things a person should check: (a) both Acts are PRS secondary copies, not gazette copies; (b) the KTCP compilation stops at Act 38 of 2015, and I did not check whether Amendment Act 10 of 2026 to the BMLTA Act changes ss.21-23; (c) the CMP is prepared by the BMLTA, a state body, not by the city government, and the city government's own duty comes through KTCP s.12(1)(b) and BMLTA s.22, with the GBA being the KTCP Planning Authority under the GBG Act 2024 (ULG-01); (d) the notification declaring the Urban Mobility Region is not in the Citation Sheet. None of these changes the YES answer on the law.

The Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 is an allied Act that makes the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) the Planning Authority under the Karnataka Town and Country Planning (KTCP) Act. It requires the GBA, through a Climate Action Cell it must set up, to formulate and implement a climate plan: the Bengaluru Climate Action and Resilience Plan (BCAP), together with plans for cutting greenhouse gas emissions. The verb is 'shall', not 'may', so this meets the 'mandate the planning authority to prepare a sustainability plan' test. (2) Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 (Karnataka Act 36 of 2025), the 'Planning Functions' sub-section (appears to be s.14(2)(a)): 'Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law ... the Greater Bengaluru Authority shall be the “Planning Authority” as defined under the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, for t

provision: Section 12 – Contents of Master Plan (substituted by Karnataka Act 1 of 2005, in force from 14.2.2005)
clause: Section 12(3); read with s.9(1) (every planning authority 'shall' prepare a master plan) and s.2(1ea)/(1eb) (definitions of Heritage Building and Heritage Precinct)
comments:
The answer is YES, which earns full marks for this sub-question (1.67). I checked the Step 2 answer against the text of ULG-02 and it holds up.

What the law says:
- Section 12(3) of the Karnataka Town and Country Planning (KTCP) Act, 1961 says the Master Plan 'shall indicate' Heritage Buildings and Heritage Precincts. It also says the plan 'shall include the regulations ... for conservation of the same'.
- This is a binding heritage-conservation part of the city master plan, which the methodology accepts in place of a separate heritage plan.
- The wording is 'shall', not 'may', so the rule against optional provisions does not apply.
- The quoted wording appears twice in ULG-02, word for word: in the consolidated s.12 text (page 32) and in the reproduced Amendment Act 1 of 2005 (page 117).
- Section 9(1) says every planning authority 'shall' prepare and publish a master plan.
- Section 13-D applies sections 9 to 12 to every revision of the master plan, so the heritage requirement also binds Revised Master Plans.

Why it applies to Bengaluru: the Step 2 evidence shows that the Greater Bengaluru Governance Act (GBA Act, ULG-01) makes the Greater Bengaluru Authority the 'Planning Authority' under the KTCP Act for the Greater Bengaluru Area. So section 12(3) governs its master plan. I did not re-read ULG-01; I relied on the Step 2 quote. The YES answer rests on section 12(3) alone.

Supporting provisions: the GBA Act's own heritage chapter (Chapter XXII, ss.296-301) adds binding duties: a heritage list, heritage regulations and a Heritage Conservation Committee. These support the answer but are not needed for it.

Things a reviewer should check:
1. ULG-02 is a PRS compilation, a secondary source, and only covers amendments up to Act 38 of 2015. Any later amendment to section 12 has not been checked against an official consolidated text. The KTCP Amendment Bill 2025 (ULG-03) is not shown to be enacted and does not touch section 12(3).
2. Step 2 inferred that the GBA planning-authority clause is section 14(2)(a); it should be confirmed against ULG-01.

Confidence is medium rather than high because the evidence is PRS-only text and the Bengaluru link needs two instruments read together (the KTCP Act and the GBA Act).

I left 'Answer' blank because the Citation Sheet has no current metropolitan or regional plan, or a validity period for one, to compare with the city-level plan. This question is about how plans work in practice. YES needs evidence that the plan periods actually overlap or nest. NO would score 0, so it needs proof that no aligned plan exists today. The sheet gives neither.

What I checked:
(1) ULG-06, SUDA DP 2035 report dated 22 Feb 2017, p.19. The State declared the Surat Metropolitan Area under the Gujarat Metropolitan Planning Committees Act, 2008 on 11/03/2016, and set up the committee the same day without its elected members. The report says the MPC draft development plan was 'not in place as on today'. This proves absence only as of Feb 2017. DP 2035 plans for the year 2035 (pp.185, 202). Earlier SUDA plans came into force in 1986 and on 15.09.2004. Section 21 of the 1976 Act requires revision every 10 years.
(2) ULG-17, Gazette Extra No.124 of 24 Mar 2025. It shows the SUDA Final Development Plan was sanctioned by Notification No. GH/V/157 of 2020, dated 08.10.2020. Step 2 lacked this date. It gives no validity period and does not mention any metropolitan plan.
(3) ULG-01 and ULG-02, Gujarat Act 14 of 2019. It inserts s.10A into the MPC Act: the State 'may' sanction an MPC draft plan, which then becomes a binding 'final development plan'. It also inserts s.19A into the 1976 Act: the appropriate authority 'shall include' the MPC plan's spatial proposals. This aligns the content of the plans, not their validity periods. It is law, not evidence of practice, and no s.10A date has been notified for Surat in the sheet.
(4) ULG-09, NITI Aayog EMP 2047. This is an advisory economic plan, not a statutory metropolitan or regional land-use plan, so I did not treat it as the regional plan.
(5) Searching the whole sheet for an MPC development plan for Surat found nothing after 2017. No ward-level or local-area plans with validity periods were found either.

A reviewer also needs to settle a method point. SUDA DP 2035 covers the SMC area itself, and the sheet has no separate SMC city plan. So it is unclear whether there are two levels of plan to compare.

Next step (RTI): ask UD&UHD Gujarat or the Surat MPC Member Secretary whether a Surat MPC development plan has been sanctioned since 2016, and its plan period. Also get the validity period stated in the SUDA DP sanction notification of 08.10.2020.

step2_answer: ANSWER: Partly. The evidence shows that one city-level plan had a committee process, but not which sectoral departments and agencies were invited. While preparing Development Plan 2035, the Surat Urban Development Authority (SUDA) set up a Core Committee and eight sub-committees with 'internal as well as external members from all fields' and held about 60 meetings. The sub-committees included SC-5 Traffic and Transportation and SC-6 Infrastructure Planning. The plan report does not list the members or the departments and agencies invited. So the methodology's test is not shown: that at least water and sewerage, traffic, electricity, transport, health and education were all invited. There is also no evidence for plans at the other levels (zone, local area or town planning scheme). | EVIDENCE: ULG-06, Development Plan 2035 report (SUDA, 22 February 2017): (1) Ch. 16.3.2, p.166: 'Following committees were formed that included internal as well as external members from all fields, to focus on key areas... Core Committee; SC-1 Basemap Preparation; SC-2 Demographical Projection and data collection; SC-3 Simplification of GDCR; SC-4 Affordable Housing and Socio economic studies; SC-5 Traffic and Transportation proposals; SC-6 Infrastructure Planning & ORR Implications; SC-7 Tapi River Alignment, CRZ Environmental Regulations; SC-8 Industry Trade & Commerce. Approximately 60 meetings were held in totality.' (2) Ch. 19.6, pp.186-187: consultations 'included experts from several Governm

chapter: 16 Stakeholders Consultation (also 2.2 Process; 19.6 Suggestions from Stakeholders)
provision: 16.3.2 Secondary Stakeholders – Consultations with Committees
comments:
I left the Answer blank. The Citation Sheet does not show a YES, and it also does not show a NO.

Why not YES: The methodology asks whether the committee for each plan level had all sectoral public departments and agencies invited, at least water and sewerage, traffic, electricity, transport, health and education. ULG-06 (SUDA Development Plan 2035 report, 22 Feb 2017) shows a Core Committee and eight sub-committees with 'internal as well as external members from all fields', and about 60 meetings. SC-5 covered Traffic and Transportation and SC-6 covered Infrastructure Planning. Ch. 19.6 adds 'experts from several Government and Semi Government institutes'. None of these passages names who sat on the committees or who was invited. The only institutions named in 16.3.1 are the Chamber of Commerce, IIA, GICEA, GIDC estate members and SVNIT. The SMC Mayor was invited only to the 22.04.2016 meeting of elected representatives. GWSSB comes up in the SC-6 suggestions only as a water supplier to villages. GPCB and the Traffic Police appear (p.161/178) only as future participants in an air-quality study. Nothing in the report shows that the electricity distribution company, traffic police, GSRTC/transport, health or education bodies were members or invitees. 'Members from all fields' is a general phrase, not proof that specific departments were invited. I also read ULG-11 (SUDA launch presentation, 03-08-2013). It lists the planned 'Expert Committees' (4 committees) with no membership. Its 'Meeting of authorities for which land is reserved', held Jan 2013, was about land acquisition, not plan deliberation. The reservation table, which names agencies such as GSRTC, GEB and PWD, lists acquiring agencies, not invitees.

Why not NO: A NO needs affirmative absence. The Citation Sheet has no committee constitution orders, membership lists or minutes of the roughly 60 DP 2035 meetings. So the gap is 'not found', not 'absent'. Records for other plan levels (town planning schemes, local area or zone plans) are not in the sheet either. ULG-12 is only a TP Scheme 59 map. ULG-09 (NITI Aayog economic master plan), ULG-10 (disaster plan), ULG-07 (parking policy) and ULG-19 (solar city plan) are not city development plans. Their committees do not include all the required sectors. ULG-01/03/04/05/14-16 are law and regulations, which are not evidence of practice.

I agree with the Step 2 answer ('Partially Answered'). It matches the source.

For the team to confirm: (1) whether SUDA's DP 2035 counts as the 'municipal/city plan' for the SMC (ULG) question. SUDA, not the SMC, prepared it under the GTPUD Act, 1976. (2) Whether the YES test needs every plan level.

Evidence needed (RTI): SUDA PIO, for the office orders constituting the Core Committee and SC-1 to SC-8, with members and minutes (2013-2016). SMC Town Planning Department PIO, for records of inter-departmental committees used in preparing TP schemes and local area plans.

question: Does the municipal/city plan include objectives on environment and heritage conservation? >:< a) Environmental Conservation
step2_answer: ANSWER: Yes. Surat's statutory city plan, SUDA's Development Plan 2035 (DP 2035), names at least two clear natural-environment and climate-resilience priorities, each with interventions. At least one of them has a measurable target. Priority 1 is more green and recreational space. The plan proposes gardens and recreational uses on land around existing talavs (ponds), a network of 'Green Streets', and a green belt around industrial zones. It sets a recreational-zone target of 46 sq.km (45.97 sq.km, 5.84% of urbanised land) by 2035. That compares with 12 sq.km in DP 2004 and 2.46 sq.km existing in 2015. Priority 2 is protecting water bodies and natural drains. The plan aims 'To preserve the water bodies and natural drains by discouraging development around water bodies' and to promote farming around them. Priority 3 is lowering flood risk. A Digital Elevation Model was laid over land use so that new residential zones sit outside flood-prone areas. Priority 4 is cutting pollution by moving polluting industries out of residential areas into a 4.35 sq.km Industrial Shift Zone. | EVIDENCE: ULG-06 DP 2035 (SUDA, report dated 22 Feb 2017). (a) Principles §19.8.3.5 'Emphasis on green development' ('Connect the gardens and open spaces and roads with a network of "Green Streets"'), §19.8.3.6 'Preserving water channels/ water bodies/ natural drains', §19.8.3.9 'Protect and enhance environmental assets' and §19.8.3.10 'Shifting of various polluting industries'. (b) §19.11.6 Recreational Z
quote: The land around e xisting Talavs are proposed for Ga rdens and Recreational uses. Garden and open spaces at the neighbourhood level can be obtained in the TP schemes. Considering the large area and future population  of SUDA region, total 46 sq.km. of recreational spaces are proposed in DP 2035 as compared to 12 sq.km. proposed in DP 2004.
chapter: Chapter 19: Proposals, Development Plan 2035 (SUDA, report dated 22 Feb 2017)
provision: §19.11.6 Recreational Zone; also §19.8.3.5, §19.8.3.6, §19.8.3.9, §19.8.3.10, residential zone proposals (report p.191), Tables 137, 138 and 154
clause: §19.11.6 (report p.198); Table 154 (report p.222)
comments:
I checked the Step 2 answer against ULG-06 (SUDA Development Plan 2035, report dated 22 Feb 2017, plan horizon 2035). Its main passages are confirmed.

1. Priorities and interventions = YES. The plan names at least two clear natural-environment and climate-resilience priorities, each with a specific action:
(a) Green space. §19.8.3.5 'Emphasis on green development' commits to connecting gardens, open spaces and roads with a network of 'Green Streets'. §19.11.6 proposes gardens and recreational uses on the land around existing talavs (ponds), with the main block of recreational land on government land at Gabheni.
(b) Water bodies. §19.8.3.6 aims 'To preserve the water bodies and natural drains by discouraging development around water bodies' and to promote farming around them.
(c) Flood risk. On report p.191, a Digital Elevation Model of the whole SUDA area was laid over the land-use map so that new residential zones sit outside flood-prone areas.
(d) Pollution. §19.8.3.10 and report p.191 move polluting industries out of residential areas, with a 4.35 sq.km Industrial Shift Zone in Tables 138 and 154.

2. Measurable targets = YES. The recreational zone has a quantified 2035 target: 46 sq.km, compared with 12.36 sq.km in DP 2004 and 2.46 sq.km existing in 2015. This rises to 5.84% of urbanised land (Tables 137 and 138).
- Correction to Step 2: Table 154 shows that the land use proposed under section 16, after villages were excluded from SUDA's area on 24.10.2016, is 39.48 sq.km of recreational zone (5.80% of urbanised land). The 45.97 sq.km figure is the section 9 draft. Either figure is a quantified target.
- SMC's own share of the recreational zone is 16.90 sq.km (Table 137).

Please confirm these points:
(i) SUDA's DP 2035 is the statutory development plan covering the SMC area, but SUDA prepared it, not SMC. Should it count as the 'municipal/city plan'?
(ii) The only measurable targets are land-allocation figures: recreational zone area and share, and the industrial shift zone. There are no targets for green cover, air quality, greenhouse gases, biodiversity or water-body restoration. If a reviewer does not accept land allocation as an outcome indicator, the measurable-targets input becomes NO and the band drops to 2.5.
(iii) The rubric mentions 'two components', but this sub-question lists only one (Natural Environment and Climate Resilience). I scored that single component against a maximum of 5.

Other points:
- I did not count the §16.4.4 (SC 7) sector-committee suggestions. They use 'should'/'promote' and are recommendations, not plan proposals.
- ULG-19 (SMC Solar City Master Plan) and ULG-10 (SMC Disaster Management Plan) are separate plans, not the city plan, so I did not rely on them.
- The Citation Sheet does not include the sanction notification of DP 2035.

Why not YES: in the parts of the NITI Aayog Economic Master Plan for the Surat Economic Region (Sept 2024, horizon 2047) that I could read, the city government (SMC) has no defined role or specific responsibilities of its own for carrying out the plan.
(a) Ch.10.1 makes the proposed SREDA 'the key responsible entity'. SMC appears only as one of 'all Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)' that would have 'official representation' in SREDA. The methodology says membership or stakeholder status like this does not qualify.
(b) Under Ch.10.1 the G-Hub Crack Unit, the DMO and the PMU carry the defined duties: coordination, KPI monitoring, resource allocation, project structuring and financing. Those duties belong to the bodies, not to SMC.
(c) In Annexure I (Tables 9-10), the SMC Municipal Commissioner sits on the State Steering Committee, which the Chief Secretary chairs. The Municipal Commissioner, Deputy Municipal Commissioner, City Engineer and Chief Town Planner sit on the G-Hub Crack Unit. The state chairs and constituted that Unit (UD&UHD Order dated 15.09.2023). This is participation by SMC officers, not a responsibility given to the city government.
(d) Ch.10.1 says the 'ICCC of Surat Smart City can be scaled up' for regional monitoring. That is permissive wording ('can'), and the Citation Sheet does not show how the Smart City SPV relates to SMC.
(e) The plan also says ULBs 'should aim for inclusive, sustainable growth' (executive summary). That is generic and not a defined responsibility.

Why not NO: the methodology would score this 0, but I cannot show affirmative absence. The project annexures name an implementing agency for each project in brackets. For example, Annexure VII item 1.1 reads 'Surat as a docking point for Cruise Tourism (GMB, Private)'. The tool only returned excerpts of Annexures IV, V, VII and VIII, so I cannot rule out SMC being named as implementing agency for a project. If it is, that could count as a specific responsibility.

I agree with the Step 2 answer (undetermined). The source supports it.

Other caveats:
- The plan covers a 6-district region, not just the city.
- Ch.10 calls its framework 'indicative' and uses 'may' throughout.
- SREDA, the DMO and the PMU are proposed, not existing bodies.
- The prerequisite UPD26a (whether a valid adopted Economic Vision Plan exists for the city) is unresolved. The Citation Sheet shows no adoption of this plan by SMC, the state or SUDA.

What would decide this: a reviewer should read the full annexure project tables in ULG-09 (Annexures IV, V, VII, VIII), checking every bracketed agency for 'SMC'. If any project names SMC as implementing agency, the answer is YES. If none does, and the reviewer accepts that membership of the state-chaired Crack Unit is not a defined role for SMC, the answer is NO.

question: Does the city have a parking policy?  >:< Is there a clear mandate in the law for a parking policy?

Karnataka law does require a parking policy for Bengaluru, but it puts that duty on the Bengaluru Metropolitan Land Transport Authority (BMLTA), not on the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) or its City Corporations. The city government is only one of the bodies BMLTA must consult. In the sources we have, neither the city's own Act (the Greater Bengaluru Governance Act) nor the Town and Country Planning Act requires or allows the city government to prepare or adopt a city-level parking policy. The rubric asks whether the T&CP Act or the Municipal Act mandates the city government (ULG) to do this. Read strictly, that points to 0. But the mandatory duty given to a separate state transport authority, together with gaps in the sources, means this needs a methodology decision. | EVIDENCE: (1) BMLTA Act, 2022 (Karnataka Act 6 of 2023, PRS republication with Amendment Act 10 of 2026 appended), s.20(1): 'The Authority shall prepare and implement the following policies ... in consultation with the Urban Transport Agencies, Urban Local Bodies ...', and the list starts with '(a) Parking policy'. The policies must be put in the public domain for feedback before they are finalised. This is a mandatory 'shall' duty, but it falls on BMLTA. Section 6 shows BMLTA is a state-level body: if the Chairperson cannot act, the Minister for Bengaluru Development, the Transport Minister or the Chief Secretary takes over. [and the levy of fees therein]'. This is a power to regulate parking places, not a duty to prepare a policy. s.459 says by-laws are drafted by the Commissioner. ss.460-462 say they are published and need State Government confirmation. The list of compulsory duties in s.63 and the parts of the list of optional duties in s.66 that I read (including s.66(8B) 'urban planning including town planning and regulation of land use') do not mention a parking policy. (1) GPMC Act 1949, text modified up to 30.11.2017 (ULG-03). The only parking provision is s.458(36).
