question: Does the city have a city-specific Development Control Regulation (DCR)?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Surat does not appear to have a separate DCR of its own. The sources show that Surat falls under Gujarat's state-wide Comprehensive General Development Control Regulations 2017 (CGDCR). That instrument does contain a table written only for Surat: Table 6.8 in Part II (Table 7.7.4 in the AUDA copy), 'Use control and F.S.I.: Category D1 SUDA', where SUDA is the Surat Urban Development Authority. It sets Surat's own floor-space-index (FSI) limits and use zones, for example the 90 m Ring Road SPD5 zone and the FSI bonus along 36 m and 45 m roads. All other rules come from the common state-wide text. Whether a Surat-specific table inside a state-wide DCR counts as a 'city-specific DCR' (score 10) or as reliance on a state-wide DCR (score 0) is a question about how to apply the method, so I have not scored it. The NA exception does not apply: the SUDA Development Plan 2035 report gives Surat's population as 4.5 million in 2011, well above one million. | EVIDENCE: (1) CGDCR 2017 Part I, Procedure Regulations (ULG-14), Reg. 1.1.3(1), Applicability: 'These regulations shall apply to all development in the entire Gujarat State'. Table 1.1 puts the Surat Urban Development Authority in Category D1 together with AUDA, GUDA, VUDA and RUDA. The Preamble says the State Government issues the regulations under s.116A read with s.122 of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 (GTPUDA). (2) CGDCR 2017, Notification GH/V/269 of 2017 dated 12 Oct 2017, AUDA copy (ULG-05):
quote: These regulations shall apply to all development in the entire Gujarat State . Different areas are grouped in different categories as specified in Table 1.1.

provision: Regulation 1.1.3 Applicability

What the sources show:
(1) Surat's development control falls under the Comprehensive General Development Control Regulations 2017 (CGDCR). This is a single instrument issued by the state government. It was made under s.116A read with s.122 of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act 1976 (GTPUDA) and the other Acts named in its Preamble. Its Reg. 1.1.3(1) says it applies to all development in the entire Gujarat State (ULG-14; also ULG-05, Notification GH/V/269 of 2017 dated 12 Oct 2017).
(2) Table 1.1 puts the Surat Urban Development Authority (SUDA) in Category D1, together with the Ahmedabad, Gandhinagar, Vadodara and Rajkot authorities (AUDA, GUDA, VUDA, RUDA).
(3) The CGDCR does have a table only for Surat: Table 6.8 in Part II (ULG-15) and Table 7.7.4 in the AUDA copy (ULG-05), 'Category D1 SUDA'. It sets Surat's own use zones and floor-space-index (FSI) limits. All other rules (procedure, building and fire) are common to the whole state.

Why no score:
- Interpretation: it is unclear whether a Surat-only table inside a state-wide DCR counts as 'a city-specific DCR is applicable' (YES, score 10) or as 'relies on a generic/state-wide DCR' (NO, score 0). The method does not settle this, so a reviewer needs to decide.
- A NO would also need affirmative absence (proof that nothing else exists), which we don't have. The Citation Sheet has no Surat Municipal Corporation (SMC) or SUDA web page saying which DCR applies, and no list from the state urban development department (UD&UHD) of CGDCR amendments or city-specific regulations. So a separate Surat DCR or local regulation cannot be ruled out.

What I checked: ULG-14 (Reg. 1.1.3, Table 1.1); ULG-17 (Gazette Extra No.124, 24 Mar 2025: proposed variation to the SUDA Final Development Plan, which was sanctioned by notification GH/V/157 of 2020 dated 08.10.2020; it says nothing about the DCR); a search of the whole Citation Sheet for a Surat-specific DCR or GDCR (only CGDCR passages came up); and the sources reviewed for the Step 2 answer (ULG-05, ULG-15, ULG-06, ULG-03).

NA does not apply: ULG-06 (the SUDA Development Plan 2035 report) gives Surat's population as about 4.5 million in 2011, well above one million.

Period: CGDCR notified 12 Oct 2017. The copies on file are hosted on the RMC and AUDA websites and may include later amendments. That it is still the version in force in 2026 is not confirmed.

step2_answer: ANSWER: The state-wide DCR for Surat, Gujarat's CGDCR 2017, does contain heritage incentives. These are tradable development rights (TDR) for heritage buildings, a parking waiver when a heritage building is reused for hotels or homes, and permitted uses in heritage areas. But the Rajkot copy (ULG-15) ties the main incentive regime to Ahmedabad. It is headed '7.6 Heritage Conservation Plan – Ahmedabad', its TDR clause is limited to the 'Heritage Area of Ahmedabad', and its Chapter 8 refers to 'the core walled city of Ahmedabad'. So the sheet does not show that the TDR or permitted-use incentives apply to Surat. Surat's planning authority, SUDA (Surat Urban Development Authority), is in category D1, and SUDA prepared Surat's Development Plan 2035. Two state-wide provisions do appear to reach Surat, and both are restrictions: buildings listed by a Heritage Conservation Committee lose the exemption from development permission for minor works, and additions or alterations in the core walled city and gamtal (old village settlement) areas must follow the Heritage Conservation Plan. The parking waiver is written in the general parking regulation (Reg. 6.15 item 21(a)). However, it applies to buildings 'identified in the Heritage Conservation Plan', and Reg. 7.6 frames that plan as Ahmedabad's. So whether the waiver applies to Surat is unclear. The answer could be score 2 if the waiver applies to Surat, or score 1 if only the restrictions do. | EVIDENCE: (1) Which rules apply to Surat

question: Does the law mandate mechanisms for monitoring ongoing construction/development projects for compliance with approved plans and permissions?   >:< Does the law mandate a system for monitoring ongoing construction/projects for possible violations?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Yes. The law that governs the city government, the Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024, covers all three elements. (1) The Commissioner has authority to inspect ongoing construction. (2) Inspection is required at defined stages: physical verification at plinth level, and physical inspection at completion before an occupancy certificate is granted. (3) The Commissioner can issue notices, direct the builder to stop work, seal the site and order demolition. The Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act s.15(4) adds a separate stop-work power for the Planning Authority. Under GBA Act s.182(2)(a) as excerpted, the Greater Bengaluru Authority is that Planning Authority. | EVIDENCE: GBA Act (ULG-01): s.239(1) 'Construction shall not be proceeded without obtaining plinth certificate', and '(a) the Commissioner or officer authorized by him, shall carryout physical verification of the building under construction'. Builders who skip the plinth certificate pay a compounding fee (s.232(2)(e), s.233(2)(d)). s.241(3): on an application for an occupancy certificate, the Additional Chief Town Planner 'shall undertake such physical inspection of the building'. s.243(2): the Commissioner 'may authorise an officer subordinate to him to conduct site inspection for verification of the construction being under taken as per sanction plan'; if the construction deviates, 'notice shall be served'. s.240(1): notice to make alterations where work departs from the sanctioned plans. s.243(3)(c): a
quote: Construction shall not be proceeded without obtaining plinth certificate. On the application made for issue of plinth certificate.– (a) the Commissioner or officer authorized by him, shall carryout physical verification of the building under construction.
chapter: Chapter on building regulation (sections 230-248), Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 (Karnataka Act 36 of 2025)
clause: s.239(1)(a) is the main quote. Supporting clauses: s.230(9) and s.243(2) (inspection), s.241(3) (completion), s.230(10), s.240(1), s.243(3)(c) and s.243(4) (notices and stop-work)
comments:
All three inputs are YES, so the score is 5. I checked each one against the ULG-01 text myself rather than copying the Step 2 answer.

(1) Authority to inspect: YES. s.230(9): the Commissioner or officers he authorises 'may undertake such periodical physical verification of buildings as necessary for the purposes of enforcing the provisions of this Act'. s.243(2): the Commissioner 'may authorise an officer subordinate to him to conduct site inspection for verification of the construction being under taken as per sanction plan'. Both are 'may' powers. But the question asks only for authority to inspect, and these sections clearly give it.

(2) Stage-wise inspection: YES. Inspection is mandatory at two stages. s.239(1): construction 'shall not be proceeded without obtaining plinth certificate', and on the application the Commissioner 'shall carryout physical verification of the building under construction'. s.241(3): on an application for an occupancy certificate, the Additional Chief Town Planner 'shall undertake such physical inspection of the building'. s.232(2)(e) charges a compounding fee for not obtaining a plinth certificate 'at the commencement of the construction'.

(3) Notices and stop-work: YES. s.230(10): the Commissioner 'shall have the power to order for the stoppage of any construction' that endangers public health or safety. s.240(1): notice to make alterations where work departs from the sanctioned plans. s.243(2): 'notice shall be served' if the construction deviates. s.243(3)(c): a provisional order that 'may also direct that until the said order is complied with the khatadar or builder shall refrain from proceeding with the building'. s.243(4): sealing 'before or after making an order of demolition or of the stoppage of the erection of any building'. The Step 2 answer also cites KTCP Act s.15(4) (ULG-02) as a further stop-work power, but the score does not depend on it.

Caveats a person should check:
(a) The question is labelled Implementation, but the Detailed Methodology only checks legal provisions. I scored it on the law. These sections are not proof that inspections happen in practice.
(b) GBA Act s.1(3) says the Act comes into force on a date the Government sets by notification. No source in the Citation Sheet gives that date. The text does include the amending Acts 60 of 2025 and 1 of 2026, which suggests the Act is operative, but neither touches these sections. If the GBA Act is not in force, the BBMP Act 2020 (ULG-19) applies. In that case the completion inspection (s.246(3)) and the stop-work order (s.248(1)) are confirmed, but a plinth-stage inspection was not found in the excerpts read.
(c) Exemptions and loopholes: the Government may exempt classes of building from the plinth certificate (s.239(2)) and the occupancy certificate (s.241(7)). If no plinth certificate is issued within 15 days, building may continue (s.239(1)(c)).
(d) ULG-01 is a PRS copy of the Gazette text, not the Gazette itself. Building bye-laws and Rules are not in the Citation Sheet.

question: Does the law mandate mechanisms for monitoring ongoing construction/development projects for compliance with approved plans and permissions?   >:< Does the law mandate a system for monitoring ongoing construction/projects for possible violations?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Yes. The law for Surat sets up a system for monitoring construction while it is under way, and all three parts of the test are met. (1) Power to inspect: the Municipal Commissioner may inspect a building at any time while it is being built, without notice (GPMC/BPMC Act s.259). CGDCR 2017 reg. 5.1.1 lets the Competent Authority inspect any time during construction, and reg. 5.1.2 says buildings with Development Permission 'shall be subject to periodic inspection'. (2) Stage-wise monitoring: the owner and architect must give notice before work starts (reg. 5.5.1, Form 10). They must report progress at set stages (reg. 5.5.3, Schedule 13, Form 11): lower basement slab, plinth, ground floor, middle storey and last storey. On receiving a progress notice, the Competent Authority has a duty, 'if found necessary', to check for departures from the sanctioned plan within 7 days. Completion must be notified and the building opened for inspection (GPMC Act s.263, Form 12). (3) Notices and stop-work orders: GPMC Act s.260 says the Commissioner 'shall' issue a show-cause notice for work begun or carried out against the rules or bye-laws. Under s.262 he may serve notice requiring contraventions to be fixed. Under s.267(1) he 'may, by written notice, require the person ... to stop the same forthwith', with police removal under s.267(2). Under the T&CP law, GTPUD Rules 1979 r.11 (Form E) require the appropriate authority to serve a notice 'to stop any development work being carried o
quote: All buildings for which Development Permission has been granted shall be subject to periodic inspection by the Competent Authority during construction. It shall be the responsibility of the Owner, the Architect on Record or Engineer on Record, and the Clerk of Works on Record for the building to report commencement, progress at various stages, and completion of construction to the Competent Authority as specified in Regulation No. 5.5.
chapter: Procedure During Construction (CGDCR 2017, Part I Procedure Regulations), read with GPMC/BPMC Act 1949 Chapter XV (Building Regulations)
clause: Reg. 5.1.2 (periodic inspection where Development Permission is granted); Schedule 13 (stages of construction); GPMC s.267(1) (stop-work notice)
comments:
I checked each of the three aspects against the source text, and all three are met. Score: 5/5.

(1) Authority to inspect: YES. GPMC Act s.259 (ULG-13, and ULG-03 as modified to 30.11.2017) says 'The Commissioner may at any time during the erection of a building ... make an inspection thereof, without giving previous notice'. CGDCR 2017 reg. 5.1.1 (ULG-05) says the Competent Authority 'reserves the right to inspect such buildings at any time during the Period of Construction'. Reg. 5.1.2 says buildings with Development Permission 'shall be subject to periodic inspection by the Competent Authority during construction'.

(2) Stage-wise inspection: YES. Reg. 5.5.1 and Form 10 require notice before work starts. Reg. 5.5.3, Schedule 13 and Form 11 require progress notices at the lower basement slab, plinth, ground floor, middle storey (buildings above 15 m) and last storey. On receiving a progress notice, the Competent Authority has a duty, 'if found necessary', to check for departures from the sanctioned plan and decide within 7 days. At completion, GPMC s.263 requires a completion notice and inspection facilities, and the CGDCR final-inspection regulation says the Competent Authority 'shall undertake final inspection' within 21 days. This covers commencement, plinth, intermediate stages and completion, as the methodology asks. Caveat: the checks mid-construction depend on owners and Persons on Record reporting each stage, and the authority checks only 'if found necessary'.

(3) Notices and stop-work: YES. GPMC s.260(1): for work begun or carried out against the rules or bye-laws, the Commissioner 'shall' issue a written show-cause notice. Under s.262 he may serve notice at any time during the work requiring contraventions to be fixed. Under s.267(1), if the work 'is being unlawfully carried on', he 'may, by written notice, require the person ... to stop the same forthwith', and s.267(2) allows removal by the police. I confirmed the wording of s.267 in both ULG-03 and ULG-13. The Step 2 answer also cites GTPUD Rules 1979 r.11 and Form E (ULG-04). I did not re-read those, and the score does not depend on them.

The Step 2 answer matches the sources. Because the inputs rest on two instruments (the CGDCR and the GPMC Act), I rated confidence medium, not high.

question: Are there provisions to penalise violating plans?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Yes, there are penal provisions, but whether they cover 'at least five heads' depends on how the heads are counted, so no score is proposed. (1) If the sub-items (1a–1i, 2a–2f, and so on) count as heads, the Karnataka Town and Country Planning (KTCP) Act alone covers at least five through a chain of sections. Section 73 penalises any work that contravenes section 14. Section 14 requires every land use, change in land use and development to conform to the Master Plan and its regulations. Section 12 says those regulations cover zoning and land use, building line (setbacks), building height, floor area ratio (FAR) and heritage conservation. Changing a building's use and building without a commencement certificate are also caught by section 14. On this reading the answer is Yes (10). (2) If only the six numbered heads count, the KTCP penalties reach only head 1 (Development Control Regulation violations) and head 5 (building work without approval). Adding the Greater Bengaluru Governance (GBA) Act brings in head 6 (fines for unauthorised advertisements and signage) and head 5 again (demolition of, and penalties for, unauthorised construction, additions and alterations). It may also bring in head 2, building code violations, because breach of building bye-laws can lead to demolition. I did not find penal provisions for NOC violations (head 3) or encroachment (head 4). On this reading five heads are not shown. | EVIDENCE: KTCP Act 1961 (PRS compilation): s.73 'Offences and
quote: does any work in contravention of the provisions of section 14;
chapter: Chapter X – Offences and Penalties, Rules and Bye-laws (read with Chapter III ss.12, 14, 15)
provision: Section 73 (read with sections 14(1), 14(2), 14 Explanation (a), 12(1)(a), 12(1)(f), 12(3))
comments:
The count is 7. That is at least five, so the answer is 'Yes'. I counted the methodology's listed items (1a–1i, 5 and so on), because it says 'at least five of the below'. I counted only the Town and Country Planning Act, as the methodology says. Source: KTCP Act 1961, PRS compilation with amendments up to Act 38 of 2015 (secondary copy). It does not show whether there were later amendments.

The penalty provision: s.73 punishes anyone who '(a) does any work in contravention of the provisions of section 14; ... (c) contravenes the conditions of the commencement certificate granted under sub-section (1) of section 15 ... (d) does any work in spite of refusal to grant a commencement certificate'. The penalty is 'imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees or with both'. If the offence continues after conviction, there is a further fine of up to Rs 250 a day.

The 7 items counted:
(1) Zoning/land use (1a). s.14(1): 'every land use, every change in land use and every development ... shall conform to the provisions of this Act, the Master Plan and the Report'. s.12(1)(a): the Master Plan includes 'zoning of land use ... together with Zoning Regulations'.
(2) Change in building use (1b). s.14 Explanation (a): 'development' includes 'the making of any material change in the use of any building or other land'.
(3)–(5) Setbacks/building line (1c), height (1d) and FAR (1e). s.12(1)(f): Master Plan 'regulations ... in regard to building line, height of the building, floor area ratio'. These are enforced through s.14(1) and s.73(a).
(6) Heritage (1g). s.12(3): the Master Plan 'shall indicate Heritage Buildings and Heritage Precincts and shall include the regulations made therein for conservation'.
(7) Building work without permits (head 5). s.14(2): no development 'except with the written permission of the Planning Authority ... contained in a commencement certificate'. s.73(d) punishes work done after a commencement certificate is refused. This covers alterations except interior-only works (s.14 Explanation (b)(i)). s.15(4) also allows stop-work orders and demolition.

Things a person should confirm:
(a) Items (1c)–(1g) are covered only by reading ss.73, 14 and 12 together. s.73 is a general penalty for breaching s.14 and the Master Plan; it does not name each item. Also, the s.12(1)(f) regulations are framed for 'areas of special control'. The strict count of items the Act names directly is 3: land use, change of use, and work without a permit. That would score below five. Please confirm the counting method.
(b) I did not count the following:
- s.76FF and the municipal regularisation provisions. They mention setback, FAR, fire and KSPCB (state pollution board) conditions, but they set regularisation fees, not penalties.
- s.76FFF, which punishes officials, not the people who break the rules.
- The GBA Act 2024 (ULG-01). It is the municipal law, not the T&CP Act. It has a fine for unauthorised advertisements (s.163 proviso) and demolition and penalties for unauthorised construction (ss.243–245). Counting it would add urban design/signage (head 6).
(c) I found no penal provisions for NOC violations (head 3) or encroachment (head 4) in the KTCP Act. That is only 'not found': the Citation Sheet does not include the KTCP Rules, the RMP-2015 zoning regulations or the building bye-laws.
(d) ULG-03 is a 2025 amendment Bill, not law in force. I did not use it.

The Step 2 answer's citations are accurate, and I agree with its sub-item reading.

question: Are there provisions to penalise violating plans?
step2_answer: ANSWER: Not determined. The question asks whether the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 (the state's Town and Country Planning Act) sets penalties under at least five of the six heads: DCR violations, building code violations, NOC violations, encroachment, work on a building without a permit, and urban design violations. The principal Act's text, where its penal and unauthorised-development sections would be, cannot be read in the Citation Sheet copy, so the heads cannot be counted. The only readable provision of the Act on enforcement is the 2017 amendment adding s.76A(8). It allows removal of works that contravene a Local Area Plan and eviction of people occupying land they are not entitled to under that plan. This covers the encroachment head and Local Area Plan contraventions only, and only for areas with a sanctioned Local Area Plan. | EVIDENCE: (1) ULG-01, Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 (PRS copy with amendments up to 14 of 2019): pp.2-86, which hold the principal Act, return no readable text. The amendment published in the Gazette (Extraordinary) of 13-04-2017 adds s.76A(8). Anyone occupying land they are not entitled to under a Local Area Plan shall surrender it within 3 months, or 'the appropriate authority shall' evict them and '(a) remove, pull down, or alter any building or other work ... which is such as contravenes the Local Area Plan', and '(b) any expenses ... shall be recovered from the person in default'. This is a
quote: For such development, considering it to unauthorised penalty , as specified in table 3.4, shall be charged in addition to other fees/ charges/ deposits etc.
chapter: CGDCR 2017 Part I (Procedure Regulations), Regulation 3 (Development Permission)
provision: Regulation 3.10 (action on unauthorised development), Table 3.4: Penalties for Undertaking Unauthorized Development

comments:
I left the count blank because the Act the method names can't be read. The method asks whether the T&CP Act, here the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, has penal provisions under at least five heads. The only copy in the Citation Sheet is ULG-01 (PRS, amended up to Gujarat Act 14 of 2019). Its pages 2-86, which hold the whole principal Act including its unauthorised-development and penalty sections, have no readable text. I searched it again and still found only the appended amendments.

A count below 5 means 'No' and scores 0. That needs affirmative absence, which isn't possible while the principal Act is unreadable. A 'Yes' also can't be shown from what can be read. The Step 2 answer ('Not determined') is supported by the sources.

What I did find, which a person should weigh against the readable Act:
(1) ULG-01, s.76A(8), added by the amendment in the Gazette (Extraordinary) of 13-04-2017. Text: 'the appropriate authority shall take following measures, namely:- (a) remove, pull down, or alter any building or other work in the area of the land included in the Local Area Plan which is such as contravenes the Local Area Plan...; (b) any expenses incurred ... shall be recovered from the person in default'. This is removal with cost recovery for encroachment and Local Area Plan breaches, and applies only where a Local Area Plan has been sanctioned. Heads: 4 (encroachment), partly 1.
(2) ULG-14 / ULG-05, CGDCR 2017 (notified 12-10-2017 under the Act). For unauthorised development the Competent Authority 'shall: a. Take suitable action which may include demolition as provided in the Act'. It may remove the work at the owner's cost and seal the building unit. Table 3.4 sets penalties for: 'a. Development commenced without taking any permission. 15', 'b. ... Development commenced which is not as per the submitted plan. 10', '... as per the submitted plan. 5', 'd. Open Uses of Land including Layout and Sub-division without taking any permission. 2'. Heads: 5 (work without permit) and partly 1 (deviation from plan).
(3) ULG-05, Schedule 16: 'Financial Penalty for Making Unauthorised Use of a Building shall be four times the Development Permission Scrutiny Fees'. Head: possibly 1b (permitted use). It is not clear whether this covers change of use or only occupation without a Building Use Permission.
(4) Outside the T&CP Act: the Municipal Act (ULG-03, GPMC Act as modified to 30-11-2017) has ss.260, 397, 399 and Chapter XXV (s.392 fines). These are demolition powers and small fines. ULG-18 (2022 Ordinance) is a regularisation law, not a penalty law.

I found no readable penal provision for building-code heads (fire, lifts, corridors), NOC heads or urban-design heads in the readable parts of the T&CP Act stack.

To do: get a readable official copy of the GTPUD Act, 1976 (its unauthorised-development and penalty sections) and decide whether CGDCR and GPMC Act penalties count toward the heads. Then count the heads and record the provision text in the scorer comments, as the scorer notes require.
